strengths: Addresses well-motivated problem of equipping latent spaces with geometric structure; bridges shape analysis and generative models
Solid theoretical foundation combining time-discrete variational geometry with inexact constraint handling via augmented Lagrangian methods
Novel denoising-based projection learning approach that generalizes beyond signed distance functions to arbitrary dimension/codimension manifolds
Flexible framework supporting multiple Riemannian metrics (Euclidean, pullback, Fisher-Rao) and different autoencoder types
Comprehensive evaluation across diverse domains (shapes, motion capture, images) with clear visual demonstrations of improvements over linear interpolation
Well-written with detailed appendix providing implementation details, parameter choices, and data generation procedures
Honest discussion of limitations and open problems
weaknesses: All experimental evaluation is qualitative/visual; lacks quantitative metrics (geodesic error vs. ground truth, path energy, smoothness, timing). No quantitative comparison with other geometric latent space methods (Arvanitidis et al. 2018, 2021, 2022)

Approximation error analysis is incomplete: O(σ²) projection error stated but propagation to geodesic errors not theoretically characterized. Error bounds for computed geodesics only demonstrated empirically on toy torus

Restrictive efficiency requirements (near-isometric embeddings or fast distance evaluation) severely limit practical applicability to general autoencoders. This fundamental limitation is underemphasized relative to its importance

Missing critical experimental elements: no ablation studies on sensitivity to K, σ, network architecture for Π_σ, or augmented Lagrangian hyperparameters; no convergence analysis for inexact implicit functions ζ_σ

Vague practical guidance: choosing σ depends on 'sampling density' with rule-of-thumb η* being 'problem-dependent'; no systematic procedure provided. Unclear how to relate desired geodesic accuracy to σ and network choices

Limited novelty in individual components: time-discrete calculus from prior work (Rumpf & Wirth 2015), projection learning adapted from existing denoising autoencoder framework. Originality is primarily in combination
Computational complexity and scalability not addressed: geodesics require nested optimization (augmented Lagrangian with BFGS inner loops); no runtimes reported or complexity analysis provided
Code availability not mentioned; essential for reproducing a computational method. Reproducibility limited to pre-trained models and public datasets
Stochastic nature of VAEs/SVAEs largely ignored despite mentioning Fisher-Rao metric; framework uses sampled deterministic points rather than proper distributional treatment
Incomplete extension to distance functions (Section 5.4): exponential map computation impossible without gradient information; only one example provided

strengths: Clear and well-motivated problem: latent manifolds lack explicit geometric structure despite widespread use
Theoretically grounded framework: properly builds on established discrete geodesic calculus (Rumpf & Wirth 2015) with principled augmented Lagrangian methods
Clever denoising-based projection learning that extends prior work (Alain & Bengio 2014) to the implicit manifold setting
Comprehensive experimental coverage across diverse data types (shells, motion capture, images, distance functions) with detailed appendices
Honest discussion of limitations including the critical near-isometric requirement and hyperparameter selection challenges
weaknesses: Critical practical limitation: method requires near-isometric encoders to work well, which defeats much of the motivation. Experiments use mostly autoencoders specifically regularized to be isometric or geometrically designed (SVAE), limiting demonstration of practical utility

Entirely qualitative experimental validation with no quantitative metrics: no comparison to ground truth geodesics, no quantitative baselines (linear interpolation, Arvanitidis et al., Sun et al.), no computational cost analysis, no metrics on path quality or curvature

Limited novelty: discrete geodesic calculus is direct application of Rumpf & Wirth (2015); projection learning is straightforward application of denoising autoencoders (Alain & Bengio 2014). Overall contribution feels incremental

Inadequate theoretical analysis of approximate projection: no error propagation analysis from Πσ to geodesic quality, σ selection is ad-hoc rather than principled, convergence theory for inexact constraints (ζσ ≠ 0) is unanalyzed despite being essential to the method

Missing practical guidance: no principled procedure for selecting σ across datasets, network architecture for Πσ varies by example without clear design principles, no sensitivity analysis or ablation studies, no comparison of computational cost vs. alternative methods

Incomplete related work positioning: insufficient differentiation from Sun et al. (2025)'s implicit representation approach, missing detailed comparison to recent latent geometry methods (Gruffaz & Sassen 2025), unclear when/why this approach is preferable to direct metric learning
VAE handling problematic: Section 5.2 treats stochastic encoders deterministically 'by slight abuse of notation,' which is concerning for a method claiming to leverage geometric structure
Self-intersection artifacts remain due to σ-limited accuracy of Πσ, limiting applicability to shape analysis and raising questions about practical utility

strengths: Well-motivated problem: Addresses the genuine gap of adding Riemannian geometric structure to autoencoder latent spaces, which is useful for shape analysis and other applications.
Robust to imperfect representations: The augmented Lagrangian method provably handles inexact constraints ζσ, making the approach practical for learned projections with inherent approximation errors.
Elegant and theoretically justified projection learning: Using denoising objectives to learn Πσ with O(σ²) error characterization and connection to Gaussian-weighted barycenters is well-motivated.

Comprehensive experimental breadth: Evaluation spans multiple autoencoder types (isometric, spherical VAE, regularized) and diverse data types (shapes, motion, images, distance functions), demonstrating generality.
Clear presentation and strong visualizations: Figure 1 effectively conveys the overall approach; mathematical exposition is generally accessible and well-organized.
Flexible metric framework: Supporting Euclidean, pullback, and information-geometric metrics provides useful flexibility for different applications.
weaknesses: Predominantly qualitative evaluation: Missing critical quantitative metrics such as (i) accuracy of computed geodesics satisfying geodesic equations, (ii) approximation error in geodesic length, and (iii) impact of projection error ζσ on final results. Parameter study confined to toy torus.

Incomplete convergence analysis for learned projections: While Rumpf & Wirth (2015) provides convergence for perfect implicit functions, this paper lacks rigorous analysis of how error in (ζσ, Dζσ) propagates to geodesic errors. Conditions for 'sufficient' approximation are unquantified.

Computational efficiency not adequately addressed: No runtime comparisons, scalability analysis, or cost breakdown (e.g., augmented Lagrangian iteration count). Claim that efficiency requires near-isometric embeddings is stated but not experimentally validated.

Ad-hoc hyperparameter selection for σ: No principled guidance for choosing σ; different values used across experiments (0.005-0.05) without justification. The O(σ²) error defect magnitude and its practical implications are not analyzed.

Informal treatment of VAEs: Stochastic encoders/decoders are sampled and treated deterministically ('by a slight abuse of notation'), discarding uncertainty structure. Suggested KL divergence approach is mentioned but not actually implemented.

Limited comparison with related work: No direct experimental comparison with Arvanitidis et al. (2018, 2021), Chen et al. (2018), or other metric learning approaches. Unclear whether this method is preferable to existing alternatives.

Limited novelty of core components: Time-discrete geodesic calculus from Rumpf & Wirth (2015), denoising projections from Alain & Bengio (2014). Main contribution is the combination with neural networks, which is useful but incremental.

Reproducibility concerns: No code availability mentioned; many hyperparameter choices lack justification; network architectures vary across experiments; convergence criteria and iteration counts inconsistently specified.

Limited practical validation: Applications confined to well-studied benchmarks; no demonstration of downstream task benefits (e.g., does geodesic interpolation improve generation vs. linear interpolation?). Unclear if practitioners would adopt over simpler baselines.
Insufficient guidance on metric selection: Section A.1 lists metric options but provides minimal guidance on which to choose for a given application, creating ambiguity for practitioners.

strengths: Novel theoretical framework: Develops a principled time-discrete geodesic calculus for implicitly defined latent manifolds, combining discrete differential geometry with learned implicit representations in a new way.
Mathematical rigor: The mathematical development is grounded in differential geometry with proper Riemannian formulations, deriving discrete geodesics from variational principles (Eqs. 1-12).
Comprehensive experimental coverage: Diverse datasets including discrete shells, motion capture, image data, and distance functions demonstrate broad applicability of the framework.
Detailed methodology: Extensive appendices provide algorithmic details (Algorithm 1), hyperparameter specifications, and implementation guidance for reproducibility.
Clear problem motivation: Effectively motivates the gap between using low-dimensional latent spaces and not explicitly exploiting their geometric structure for practical operations.
Multiple visualization examples: Figures clearly demonstrate that geodesic interpolation can follow manifold structure better than linear interpolation (e.g., Figures 5, 6, 9).
weaknesses: Missing convergence analysis: No formal convergence guarantees for the discrete geodesic computation or augmented Lagrangian method; approximation error bounds as a function of discretization parameters are absent.

Insufficient quantitative evaluation: Evaluation relies predominantly on visual inspection rather than numerical metrics; limited comparison against other geometric methods (comparisons confined to appendix Section C).

Lack of computational complexity analysis: Training overhead of the projection network and computational cost comparison to linear interpolation not systematically addressed; scalability to higher-dimensional latent spaces unclear.
Heavy dependence on learned projection: Framework critically depends on accurate learning of Π_σ, but failure modes and quality degradation scenarios are not thoroughly analyzed.

Hyperparameter sensitivity without principled selection: Figures 10-11 demonstrate sensitivity to σ and architecture choices, but limited guidance provided for hyperparameter selection beyond rules of thumb.

Limited practical impact demonstration: Beyond shape interpolation, applications remain unclear; for some tasks (e.g., Figures 5, 9), linear interpolation produces qualitatively similar results, questioning when this method is necessary.
Restricted experimental scope: All experiments use relatively low-dimensional latent spaces (≤84 dimensions); applicability to very high-dimensional manifolds unexplored.
Presentation issues: Dense mathematical notation; key results and comparisons relegated to appendices; insufficient clarity on which contributions are novel versus applying existing techniques.

strengths: Novel application of discrete geodesic calculus to learned implicit latent manifolds, combining Riemannian geometry with neural network-based autoencoders
Mathematically principled framework building on established theory (Rumpf & Wirth 2015)
Comprehensive experimental evaluation across three different autoencoder architectures (discrete shells, spherical VAE, image autoencoders) with diverse datasets
Creative approach to learning approximate projections via denoising-based loss functional (Eq. 13)
Clear motivation, good presentation quality, and effective use of visualizations
Thorough appendices with algorithm details, metric discussions, and experimental setup descriptions
weaknesses: Critical theory-practice gap: Theoretical convergence guarantees assume exact manifold projections (exact Π), but practical implementation uses learned approximate projections (Π_σ via neural networks). No theoretical justification provided for why this approximation preserves geometric properties or maintains convergence guarantees

Absence of convergence analysis for the discrete geodesic scheme under approximate projection: convergence as K→∞ is only proven for exact constraints; behavior with learned projections and penalty enforcement (Eq. 9) is unanalyzed

Lack of quantitative evaluation metrics: Almost all comparisons are qualitative/visual inspections. No numerical metrics for interpolation quality (e.g., Fréchet distance, geodesic distortion), making it impossible to assess improvements rigorously
Modest empirical improvements: Visual improvements over linear interpolation are often subtle (e.g., Figures 5, 16-18); gains don't clearly justify the added complexity and computational cost
Narrow applicability: Method only useful for specialized scenarios with autoencoders featuring learned implicit geometry and low-dimensional latent spaces (6D-24D tested)
No principled parameter selection guidelines: Critical parameters (σ, α, K) appear to be chosen ad-hoc despite Figure 10-11 showing high sensitivity to σ

Insufficient comparison with related work: Limited comparison with recent implicit manifold methods (Arvanitidis et al. 2022, Pouplin et al.); marginal differences with existing approaches in Figure 16-18
Unresolved issues with negatively-curved spaces (Figure 4): Method diverges in these regions; limitation acknowledged but not addressed, restricting method generality
Reproducibility concerns: No code availability mentioned; scattered implementation details; random seeds and initialization strategies not specified
Missing scalability analysis: No evaluation of computational complexity or convergence speed as K increases; only low-dimensional latent spaces tested

strengths: Well-motivated problem addressing a genuine gap in geometric tools for implicit autoencoder latent manifolds
Rigorous mathematical framework with properly formulated discrete geodesic calculus using constrained optimization
General approach accommodating multiple Riemannian metrics and extending to distance function representations
Comprehensive experimental validation across five diverse applications with convincing visual evidence of quality improvements
Clear algorithmic specification and thorough documentation of implementation details in appendices
Honest treatment of method limitations and discussion of parameter sensitivity (σ effects shown in Figures 10-11)
Solid theoretical justification connecting projection learning to denoising objectives through prior work
weaknesses: Limited quantitative evaluation—results are primarily visual with no metrics comparing geodesic vs. linear interpolation on reconstruction quality or distance preservation
Practical benefits unclear—no downstream task improvements or scenarios demonstrating when geodesics substantially outperform simpler alternatives
Incremental novelty combining established techniques (discrete geodesic calculus, denoising-based projections, implicit representations) rather than introducing fundamental innovations

Incomplete theoretical analysis: convergence guarantees for learned projection Π_σ as noise σ→0 not analyzed, discretization error characterization missing, constraint satisfaction only enforced via penalties
Computational cost not systematically addressed despite geodesic computation appearing substantially more expensive than linear interpolation
Limited failure mode analysis with only brief mention of numerical instabilities in negatively curved regions
Hyperparameter sensitivity incompletely characterized beyond σ studies—unclear effects of α, μ₀, λ parameters
Overstated claims about independence from autoencoder quality—results fundamentally depend on learned manifold structure
Missing code release and some implementation details (exact architectures for all experiments) reducing reproducibility
